pedagogy.summary: Dividing a fraction by a fraction is where the general 'keep-change-flip' (invert-and-multiply) procedure arrives — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6. The danger is that it is learned as a meaningless ritual: IES documents that most students (and many teachers) cannot explain why inverting works, and consequently misapply it — not inverting either fraction (→ 8/15), inverting the wrong fraction, or inverting both. The teaching goal is to bind the rule to meaning: keep the measurement reading ('how many 4/5s fit in 2/3?', a bit less than one), model it, and — for the strongest pupils — derive the rule (multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1). Estimation guards the result.
bestPractices: Anchor the procedure in the measurement meaning — 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3?' — modelled on a common-denominator bar or number line, so the flipped rule has something to explain
Derive invert-and-multiply rather than assert it (IES): multiply dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor; the divisor becomes 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal
Drill the STRUCTURE of the rule against its misapplications — flip ONLY the divisor (the second fraction), keep the first, change ÷ to × — by contrasting correct vs 8/15 / wrong-flip worked examples
Estimate first: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 is close to 2/3 ÷ 1, so a little more than 2/3 — catches an inverted-wrong-fraction blunder
Connect to the common-denominator method (2/3 = 10/15, 4/5 = 12/15, so 10 ÷ 12 = 10/12 = 5/6) so pupils see the rule and the meaning agree
keyRepresentations: Common-denominator bar/number line showing how many divisor-lengths fit in the dividend
Keep-change-flip written with only the SECOND fraction inverted, colour-coded
Estimation number line placing the quotient near 2/3
commonMisconceptions: Does not invert either fraction — just multiplies: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 8/15 (IES)
Inverts the wrong fraction — flips the dividend: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 3/2 × 4/5 (IES)
Applies keep-change-flip correctly but as a rote rule — cannot model it, justify the flip, or judge if the answer is reasonable

learn.summary: Dividing a fraction by a fraction is where invert-and-multiply ('keep-change-flip') completes: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6. The risk is that it becomes a meaningless ritual — students fail to invert either fraction (→ 8/15), invert the wrong fraction, or invert both. The teaching goal is to bind the rule to meaning: read it as a measurement ('how many 4/5s fit into 2/3?' — a bit less than one), model that, contrast correct and misapplied methods, derive why only the divisor inverts, and use estimation to guard the answer.

activities.title: Measure it and run the rule side by side
feedback: If a learner lays the 4/5 bars and sees more than one fits, re-check the bar lengths against a common-denominator scale (2/3 = 10/15, 4/5 = 12/15): since 12/15 > 10/15, less than one 4/5 fits.
If the rule and the measurement disagree, check which fraction was flipped — only the second (the divisor) should invert; the first stays 2/3.

When the wrong-flip answer 6/5 appears, point out that dividing 2/3 by something only a little less than 1 should give only a little more than 2/3, and the measurement showed less than one whole 4/5 fits (an answer below 1); 6/5 is greater than 1 and nearly double 2/3, so it cannot be right.
activities.rationale: Grounding invert-and-multiply in the measurement meaning and a common-denominator view (10/15 ÷ 12/15 = 10/12) gives the flip something concrete to explain, and making a wrong flip visibly diverge from the measured value targets the exact documented misapplications.
sourceClaims: Students commonly misapply invert-and-multiply: not inverting either fraction (2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 8/15), inverting the wrong fraction (3/2 × 4/5), or inverting both (3/2 × 5/4); such errors reflect a lack of conceptual understanding of why the procedure works

Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide fractions by fractions, including using visual fraction models and the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g. via common denominators)
learnerActions: Take a bar representing 2/3 and lay 4/5-length bars into it; find that not even one whole 4/5 fits, and read how much of a 4/5 does fit (about 5/6 of one).
Alongside, run keep-change-flip: keep 2/3, change ÷ to ×, flip ONLY the 4/5 to 5/4, and compute 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.
Confirm the measured amount (5/6 of a 4/5 fits) and the rule's answer (5/6) agree.
Deliberately flip the wrong fraction (3/2 × 4/5 = 6/5) or both (3/2 × 5/4 = 15/8) and compare each result to the measured 5/6 — notice how far each wrong flip lands from what you measured.
activities.intendedInsight: Inverting the divisor is not an arbitrary trick: the rule's answer matches the measured 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3', and flipping the dividend or both pulls the answer away from that measured amount.

activities.title: Derive why only the divisor inverts
feedback: If a learner inverts the dividend too, show that doing so changes the value of the dividend, whereas the derivation only ever turns the divisor into 1 and keeps the dividend as it was.
If the step 4/5 × 5/4 = 1 is unclear, have them multiply numerators and denominators: (4×5)/(5×4) = 20/20 = 1.
activities.rationale: The reciprocal derivation gives a justification stronger pupils can own, directly countering the 'it's just a rule' and 'invert both' errors.
sourceClaims: Invert-and-multiply can be DERIVED, not asserted: multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal; visual models and estimation should accompany the procedure to make it meaningful
learnerActions: Start from 2/3 ÷ 4/5 and multiply both the dividend and the divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor, 5/4: (2/3 × 5/4) ÷ (4/5 × 5/4).
State in your own words why the dividend 2/3 is left untouched and only the divisor is turned into 1.
Explain, using this derivation, why flipping both fractions (3/2 × 5/4) is wrong — the dividend was never inverted.
activities.intendedInsight: Invert-and-multiply can be derived rather than asserted: multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal, which is why only the divisor flips.

activities.title: Estimate before you compute
feedback: If a learner accepts 8/15, ask: dividing by something just under 1 should give a bit MORE than 2/3, but 8/15 is LESS than 2/3 (8/15 vs 10/15) — so the method must be wrong.
Reinforce that dividing a positive number by a positive number less than 1 produces a result larger than the dividend.
activities.rationale: Estimation is a documented guard that should accompany the procedure to keep it meaningful and reasonable.
sourceClaims: Invert-and-multiply can be DERIVED, not asserted: multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal; visual models and estimation should accompany the procedure to make it meaningful
learnerActions: Before calculating 2/3 ÷ 4/5, note that 4/5 is close to 1, so 2/3 ÷ 4/5 should be close to 2/3 ÷ 1 = 2/3, and a bit more than 2/3 because you are dividing by a little less than 1.
After computing, check whether your answer (5/6) is more than 2/3 (2/3 = 10/15, 5/6 ≈ 12.5/15) — it is.
Use the estimate to reject answers like 6/5 (too big) or 8/15 (less than 2/3, wrong direction).
activities.intendedInsight: A quick estimate of the expected size catches inverted-wrong-fraction and no-flip blunders before they are accepted.

activities.title: Diagnose the method, not just the answer
feedback: Answer 8/15 with no flip: return to the measurement meaning and derivation — ÷ 4/5 must undo multiplying by 4/5, so the divisor inverts.
Answer 6/5 with the dividend flipped: keep the FIRST, flip only the SECOND; use the estimate (answer near but a bit more than 2/3) to flag 6/5 as impossible.
Answer 15/8 with both flipped: only dividing BY the divisor needs undoing, so only the divisor flips — walk the derivation where the dividend is untouched.
Correct 5/6 but a blank or 'that's just the rule' model/story: build the 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3' model alongside the rule and require an estimate on the next problem.
activities.rationale: Watching the method reveals the precise way invert-and-multiply fails — each wrong answer names a specific documented misapplication — and requiring a model or story elicits a production that recognition alone does not.
sourceClaims: Students commonly misapply invert-and-multiply: not inverting either fraction (2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 8/15), inverting the wrong fraction (3/2 × 4/5), or inverting both (3/2 × 5/4); such errors reflect a lack of conceptual understanding of why the procedure works
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 ÷ 4/5 showing every step of the method.
Then draw a picture or tell a story that shows what 2/3 ÷ 4/5 actually means.
Transfer the method to a new case, e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4, and say whether the answer is bigger or smaller than 1/2 and why.
Match each wrong result — 8/15, 6/5, 15/8 — to the mistake that produced it (no flip, wrong fraction flipped, both flipped).
activities.intendedInsight: Owning fraction division means producing the answer, modelling or story-ing the division, justifying why only the divisor flips, and judging the answer's reasonableness — not just reciting the steps.

activities.title: Defend each step to a questioner
feedback: If the learner can only say 'that's the rule', redirect them to the derivation (multiply dividend and divisor by 5/4 so the divisor becomes 1) or the measurement model.
Accept a justification only when it explains why the dividend is left unchanged.
activities.rationale: A questioning dialogue can surface whether a correct answer rests on understanding or ritual, complementing the visual modelling activities; this is a proposed, untested teaching move.
learnerActions: Present each step of 2/3 ÷ 4/5 to a partner or tutor who keeps asking 'why?' and refuses 'because that's the rule' as an answer.
Justify why the division becomes a multiplication, why only the second fraction flips, and why 5/6 is reasonable.
Answer the follow-up: how would the answer change if you flipped the other fraction instead?
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed for justification can expose a merely rote rule and can push the learner to connect the procedure to the reciprocal derivation and the measurement meaning.

constraints: The target objective is procedural fluency WITH meaning: a learner must model or story the division, justify why only the divisor inverts, and estimate the answer — producing 5/6 alone is not sufficient.
Colour-coding or locking only the second fraction when it flips is a helpful scaffold, but learners must eventually apply the rule without the visual aid.

A matching/selection task can diagnose which misapplication a learner makes and can be used during teaching, but recognising a correct answer does not elicit independent construction of a model or a story — pair it with open working and a modelling demand.

A static worked example (tap-to-reveal steps, 'why only the second flips' flap) supports reading the procedure but does not let the learner test a wrong flip or model a new case; use it as a reference, not the primary task.
Estimation is a check, not the method; use it to flag impossible answers, not to replace exact computation.
Fraction ÷ fraction is a length/quantity comparison that is naturally represented on a bar or number line; a flat model is adequate here, and this is not evidence that any other medium would fail.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The quotient 5/6 is simultaneously a bit LESS than one whole 4/5 (the measurement reading, since 2/3 < 4/5) and a bit MORE than 2/3 (the estimation reading, since dividing by 4/5 < 1 enlarges the dividend); both statements are consistent, not contradictory.

The source labels invert-and-multiply as the general procedure arriving at fraction ÷ fraction; this rewrite presents it as derivable and measurable rather than as the only valid method — the common-denominator route (10/15 ÷ 12/15 = 10/12) is retained as an equivalent approach.

The IES claim is cited as support for the general misapplication pattern and the derivation principle; it does not establish that any specific activity here has been tested for efficacy. The Common Core citation (6.NS.1) is marked verified:false in the source.

The 'Defend each step to a questioner' activity has sourceClaims set to [] because no cited source directly supports Socratic questioning as a teaching/diagnostic method; it is retained only as a conservative, qualified proposal.

probeDeeper: Why does flipping the second fraction and multiplying give the right answer — convince me it isn't just a trick.
Is 5/6 bigger or smaller than 2/3, and does that make sense for dividing by 4/5 (which is nearly 1)?
Try 1/2 ÷ 1/4 with your method — is the answer bigger or smaller than 1/2, and why?
Which single fraction gets flipped, and how would the answer change if you flipped the other one instead?
assess.correctAnswer: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6. Meaning: 'how many 4/5s fit into 2/3?' — a bit less than one whole 4/5 fits, namely 5/6 of it. (Or common denominators: 10/15 ÷ 12/15 = 10/12 = 5/6.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not invert either fraction — just multiplies straight across: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the measurement meaning and the reciprocal derivation — show that ÷ 4/5 must undo multiplying by 4/5, so the divisor is inverted; contrast 8/15 with the measured 5/6
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Working shows a direct multiplication with no flip; answer 8/15

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverts the WRONG fraction — flips the dividend instead of the divisor: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 3/2 × 4/5 = 6/5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Colour-lock the rule — keep the FIRST, flip only the SECOND (the divisor) — and use estimation (answer should be near 2/3) to flag 6/5 as impossible; re-derive which fraction inverts
errorPatterns.revealedBy: First fraction is inverted in the working; answer 6/5 (bigger than the dividend, wrong direction)

errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that only the operation of dividing BY the divisor needs undoing, so only the divisor flips; walk the reciprocal derivation where the DIVIDEND is untouched
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Both fractions flipped in the working; answer 15/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies keep-change-flip correctly to 5/6 but as pure ritual — cannot draw a model, tell a matching story, or explain why the flip works or whether 5/6 is reasonable
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3' model alongside the rule so the procedure gains meaning; require an estimate before computing on the next problem
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct 5/6 but the modelling/story task is blank, wrong, or 'that's just the rule'; no estimation offered

responseLevels.gap: Does not invert, inverts the wrong fraction, or inverts both — the procedure is misapplied and no meaning is available.
responseLevels.full: Computes 5/6 correctly AND grounds it — models or stories 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3', explains (or derives via the reciprocal) why invert-and-multiply works, estimates the answer's size, and transfers the method reliably to a new fraction ÷ fraction case.
responseLevels.partial: Keeps-changes-flips correctly to 5/6 but purely by rule — cannot model the division, tell a matching story, justify why only the divisor flips, or estimate whether the answer is reasonable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 2/3 ÷ 4/5, showing every step of your method. Then draw a picture or tell a story that shows what 2/3 ÷ 4/5 actually means.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the METHOD catches the exact way the invert-and-multiply rule fails, which a bare answer would hide. A child who does not invert lands on 8/15; one who flips the dividend gets 6/5; one who flips both also errs — each wrong answer names the precise misapplication (all documented by IES). And the demand to MODEL or story the division separates the child who owns the meaning (can show 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3') from the one running a rote ritual — the latter computes 5/6 but cannot represent it or say why only the second fraction flips.
